chapters.title: Chapter 3: Understanding Your Income and Tax

lessons.title: Old vs New Tax Regime: Choosing the Right One for Your Salary

body.text: Deductions are not savings. They only matter if they cut your tax by more than the new regime's lower rates already do. For most salaried Indians today, they don't. Your own numbers are the only way to know which side of that line you are on.

markDefs.definition: The concessional tax regime with lower slab rates and very few deductions, governed by Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 115BAC of the 1961 Act). It is the default for individuals.

children.text: India runs two parallel ways of computing income tax for individuals. The

, under Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 115BAC of the Income-tax Act, 1961), is the default. It offers lower rates and a larger rebate, but takes away most exemptions and deductions. The old regime keeps HRA, 80C, 80D and home loan interest, but at higher rates. You have to actively opt out of the new regime to use the old one.

children.text: The only honest way to compare is to compute both. Here are three salaried employees, all below 60, for FY 2025-26. The deductions listed are those available in the old regime, over and above the standard deduction.

cells: Ankit, analyst at a Pune startup
Sneha, manager at an IT firm in Bengaluru
Rajesh, senior vice president at a bank in Mumbai

body.title: Show me the full working for Sneha and Rajesh

cells: Less: HRA exemption ₹4,00,000, interest on loan for his family home in Nashik ₹2,00,000, 80C ₹1,50,000, 80D ₹75,000, 80CCD(1B) ₹50,000, 80G ₹25,000

body.text: Look at Sneha. She claims over ₹5 lakh of deductions, including a large HRA exemption and a health policy for her parents, and still pays ₹39,520 more in the old regime. Having deductions is not the test. Having enough of them to beat the new regime's lower rates is.

children.text: The Breakeven: How Many Deductions Do You Need?

For each salary level, there is a total of old regime deductions at which both regimes give the same tax. Below it, the new regime wins. Above it, the old regime wins. The chart shows this breakeven for a salaried individual below 60, counting deductions beyond the standard deduction.

body.title: Old Regime Deductions Needed to Break Even, FY 2025-26

body.text: Why does the line dip at ₹15 lakh? Up to a salary of ₹12.75 lakh, the new regime rebate makes tax nil, so the old regime needs enormous deductions just to reach zero. Just past that point, the rebate disappears and the new regime starts charging tax, so the bar drops. Beyond ₹24 lakh of taxable income both regimes charge 30% at the margin, and the breakeven settles at about ₹8 lakh. Rules of thumb break at exactly the salaries where people most want one, so run the numbers.

body.label: Breakeven at High Salaries
body.context: Above a salary of about ₹25 lakh, you need roughly ₹8 lakh of old regime deductions beyond the standard deduction before the old regime saves you anything.

body.title: A Close Call in Chennai
body.prompt: Farhan, 33, earns a salary of ₹15,00,000 in Chennai. In the old regime he can claim ₹5,25,000 of deductions beyond the standard deduction: HRA exemption ₹3,00,000, 80C ₹1,50,000, 80D ₹25,000 and 80CCD(1B) ₹50,000. Compute his total tax, including cess, under both regimes. By how much does the better regime reduce his tax?

body.title: Marginal relief: what happens just above ₹12 lakh

children.text: Without a safeguard, earning ₹1 more than ₹12 lakh of taxable income would suddenly cost you over ₹60,000. Marginal relief prevents this: in the new regime, the tax on income slightly above ₹12 lakh cannot exceed the amount by which the income exceeds ₹12 lakh. Take taxable income of ₹12,10,000. Slab tax is ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + 15% of ₹10,000 = ₹61,500. With marginal relief, tax is capped at ₹10,000, plus 4% cess of ₹400, so ₹10,400. The relief fades out as income rises and stops mattering at about ₹12.7 lakh of taxable income. Also note that the rebate does not cover tax on income taxed at special rates, like short-term gains on listed shares, so that tax can be payable even when your total income is below ₹12 lakh.

body.text: Miss the due date and you lose the choice. A salaried person who files a belated return is taxed under the new regime, whatever deductions they had planned to claim. For Rajesh, filing in September instead of July would cost ₹31,200 in extra tax, on top of the late fee. If the old regime works for you, the due date is a hard deadline.

body.title: Can Pooja Change Her Mind?
body.question: In April 2025, Pooja told her employer in Gurugram to deduct TDS under the new regime. When preparing her ITR in July 2026, she finds the old regime would save her ₹22,000. She has only salary and interest income. What can she do?
options: Nothing, since the choice given to her employer is final for the year
Choose the old regime in her ITR, provided she files by 31 July 2026
Choose the old regime, but only by filing Form 10-IEA first
Choose the old regime in a belated return filed any time before 31 December 2026
body.explanation: For someone without business income, the declaration to the employer only decides monthly TDS. The real choice is made in the ITR, and she can pick the old regime as long as the return is filed by the due date. Form 10-IEA is needed only by people with business or professional income. A belated return would lock her into the new regime.

body.title: The Rebate Limit
body.textWithBlank: In the new regime for FY 2025-26, a resident individual with total income up to ₹___ lakh pays no tax on normal income, thanks to the rebate.
body.explanation: The rebate under Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 87A of the 1961 Act) is up to ₹60,000 for total income up to ₹12 lakh. For a salaried person, add the ₹75,000 standard deduction, and a salary of ₹12,75,000 attracts no tax.

body.title: The Salaried Trader
body.scenario: Rohan, 30, earns a salary of ₹22,00,000 at a consulting firm in Delhi and also trades futures and options on Zerodha, which gave him a small business profit in FY 2025-26. He has a home loan on the flat he lives in and claims 80C and 80D, and his CA says the old regime saves him about ₹25,000. His friend, a salaried employee with no trading income, says you can simply tick the old regime box in the ITR every year. Rohan plans to file in late July 2026.
body.prompt: Is his friend's advice right for Rohan? What does he need to do, and what should he keep in mind for future years?
body.modelAnswer: No. Rohan's F&O profit is business income, so the simpler every-year choice available to purely salaried people does not apply to him. To use the old regime, he must file Form 10-IEA to opt out of the new regime by the due date of his return. Since he has business income, ITR-3 applies, and he should confirm that due date on the portal rather than assume 31 July. The bigger catch is flexibility. Having opted out, he can return to the new regime only once while he has business income. If his deductions shrink later, for example when the home loan is repaid, he can switch back to the new regime, but after that he loses the option to move to the old regime again. He should weigh that before opting out for a ₹25,000 saving.

body.title: Pick Your Regime in Five Steps
steps: Add up your gross salary and other income for FY 2025-26
List every old regime deduction and exemption you genuinely qualify for, with proofs: HRA, 80C, 80D, 80CCD(1B), home loan interest, 80G
Compute tax under both regimes, including cess, using the portal's tax calculator or the working in this lesson
Check whether you have any business or professional income, including F&O, which changes the switching rules
If the old regime wins, file by the due date, and add Form 10-IEA first if you have business income

points: The new regime under Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 115BAC of the 1961 Act) is the default, with lower rates, a ₹75,000 standard deduction and very few other deductions
The rebate under Section 156 (87A of the 1961 Act) makes total income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free in the new regime, so salaries up to ₹12.75 lakh pay nil tax
The old regime keeps HRA, 80C, 80D, 80CCD(1B) and home loan interest, but only wins when those deductions exceed a breakeven that is about ₹8 lakh at high salaries
The breakeven is not a straight line, so compute both regimes for your own numbers instead of relying on a rule of thumb
Without business income, you choose the regime in the ITR every year, but only in a return filed by the due date; a belated return means the new regime
With business or professional income, including F&O, you opt out using Form 10-IEA by the due date and can switch back to the new regime only once

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Examples are simplified for resident individuals below 60 with no surcharge. Slab rates, rebates, deductions and switching rules reflect the position for FY 2025-26 at the time of writing and can change with each Finance Act. Compute your own tax on the Income Tax Department's portal or consult a qualified tax professional.
